source.title: Feature Starvation as Geometric Instability in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Faris Chaudhry; Keisuke Yano; Anthea Monod

record.tranche_reason: The paper trains sparse autoencoders on real LLM activations and measures sparse-code reconstruction and feature utilization, bearing on V4 through a different method and measures from the original toy-model study.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses the superposition hypothesis and cites Toy Models of Superposition, but does not test its sparsity-dependent transition or regular toy-model geometry. It reports no human evaluation of whether SAE latents are semantic features and no stability or canonical-unit test. The described downstream reconstruction-patching protocol has no reported outcome in the supplied text. Hyperparameter values and cited results were not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE-architecture methods paper. It assumes the superposition/SAE framing and compares its AEN-SAE against TopK on dead features, explained variance, coherence and utilization. It never tests whether the models superpose features, whether real sparse features exist, or whether SAE latents are the model's units. Explained variance of its own SAE versus a baseline is method performance, not evidence for V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors frame starvation as coherence-induced geometric instability. They claim AEN-SAE mitigates it without heuristics, at some cost in explained variance, and admit 40–50% inactive at 8B. Their text does not acknowledge that at Pythia ℓ0≈16 AEN has more dead neurons than TopK (6.6% vs 2.3%).
record.recipe_differences: The original source studies toy-model superposition geometry; this paper trains and compares SAE architectures on synthetic sparse codes and real LLM activations, focusing on starvation, reconstruction, and dictionary diagnostics.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with SAE architecture, target ℓ0, and synthetic dictionary coherence. AEN's utilization and reconstruction trade-offs differ between Pythia 70M and Llama 3.1 8B.

fits_no_version.finding: Without auxiliary losses, TopK SAEs on Llama 3.1 8B leave 80–88% of a 131k dictionary dead, with max decoder coherence 1.000. AEN-SAE still leaves 39–55% dead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionary utilization and redundancy depend strongly on architecture; large SAEs can collapse onto near-duplicate latents.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic coherent dictionary (ρ=0.9), TopK leaves ~97% of SAE latents dead versus ~41% for AEN-SAE. Explained variance is 0.47–0.67.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary coherence limits SAE recovery of ground-truth sparse codes.

record.problems: LLM reconstruction and dictionary statistics do not validate the semantic identity or completeness of recovered features. The paper reports no human-centered interpretability assessment, which it lists as future work. Llama table values have no reported uncertainty; downstream reconstruction-patching outcomes are not present in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional Table 2 and Table 4 measures, including achieved ℓ0, MSE, and p50 coherence, and Table 1 shrinkage; these were omitted to keep the record within 60 rows and prioritize dead-feature rates, explained variance, and key geometry or utilization diagnostics. Qualitative low-coherence results and narrative-only metrics were also omitted.

untested.parts: No toy model of superposition; the spiked synthetic model tests SAE recovery of a given dictionary, not how networks store features.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Does not test whether LLM activations contain recoverable sparse features. Only SAE-architecture performance is compared; no interpretability evaluation.
No completeness, stability or canonicality test of SAE features. Dead-feature rates are optimization diagnostics.
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to T4: every LLM result is the authors' SAE vs a TopK baseline (without auxiliary loss), so it bears on SAE engineering, not on superposition. The p90 coherence in the text (0.516) disagrees with Table 2 (0.628). Downstream CE/KL patching is described but not reported.

versions.untested_parts: No test of a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry of overlapping, nearly orthogonal feature directions.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from competition for limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Measures sparse SAE reconstruction and dictionary utilization on LLM activations, but does not establish that recovered latents correspond to true or semantically interpretable model features.
No test of SAE features being complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multi-dimensional features.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia 70M and Llama 3.1 8B; sparse SAE activation reconstruction
reader_labels.reason: Sparse dictionaries reconstruct real-model activations with reported explained variance, although this does not validate individual latents as semantic features (P3, P4, P11, P12, P19, P20, L3, L4, L11, L12, L19, L20).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: AEN leaves 39.3%–55.4% of features dead at the tested target sparsities, and its explained variance is lower than Top-K in each comparison (L2, L4, L10, L12, L18, L20).
